intro: Every day the dice roll a premise and a dozen constraints, and the game has to honour all of them. Tonight's roll was seed 3391490606: a very polite castle, planting rainbows, out of revenge. Here is how that became Form T-1.

rolls.became: Castle Pardon, which apologises for everything, including its own revenge. It flies a flag that says SORRY. It does not say what for.
A rainbow lobbed from the tower comes down feet first and takes root, and the grey glass under it turns to colour. Planted rainbows stay, as little arches on every plot.
Light plus rain. The castle's stained-glass windows split the light (every window you buy makes the rainbows wider) and Spout, the gargoyle waterspout, supplies the rain.

Castles have always lobbed things at their neighbours. This one pulls back, aims and lets go, siege-engine style, except the ammunition is courtesy. The further the light reaches, the further you can throw.
One hundred thousand grey acres, counted down by the handful: a rainbow plants 1 acre at first and about 25 by the end.
Baron Brume complained that the castle was 'too colourful, an eyesore', and had its upkeep grant cut. The politest revenge there is: make his estate exactly as colourful as the castle.
Three crowns a month. Windows, taller towers and Spout's wage (one bucket of rainwater a week) all cost money, so the castle takes paid orders.
Baron B. Brume (brume is an old word for mist), and Brume Hall on its grey hill at the far end of the estate.
About an hour and a half, over a sitting or two. Spout keeps throwing while you're away, at a reduced rate.

rolls.value: orders with deadlines (fill contracts for rewards)
rolls.became: Brume's own tenants want colour too, but Estate Regulation 1 forbids paint, and a rainbow isn't paint. They pin orders to their plots, a rainbow over the sad pig by Thursday, with a fee and a deadline. Orders are the castle's only real income.

rolls.value: the number goes down: an incremental in reverse
rolls.became: The big number is grey acres, and it only goes down: the Turnip Fields, the Orchard, Brumewick, the Moor, Brume Hall. Reaching each new stretch of the estate costs crowns (a taller tower, a rose window, a decorative trebuchet).

Spout stamps every order APPROVED or DECLINED. Once he's on the payroll he throws the approved ones himself, and the dutiful ones are what he approves of: funerals, retirements, drainage ditches. Weddings are vulgar. The festive ones he declines carry a surcharge, so they're yours to land by hand.
Everything is in triplicate: one (1) rainbow, received with thanks, withdrawn with regret and on file. Brume objects to each region in writing as it turns, a little less strongly every time.
The whole scene is leaded glass: quarries of sky, a mosaic castle, and an estate of diamond panes that swap the Baron's slate for the castle's warm glass one acre at a time.
Nyx8 has two night blues and a slate for the Baron, and cream, tan, rose, mauve and plum for the castle. A rainbow in this palette is a muted dusk rainbow, which suits a castle this sorry.

A polite village-band polka in D dorian: tuba oom-pah, accordion on the off-beats, a clarinet that joins in Brumewick. It fills out as the light reaches further. Every chime and fanfare is on the same scale.
No calendar nod today. Just rainbows, in triplicate.

rolls.value: hand it all over to someone else
rolls.became: When the last grey acre is gone, the castle signs Form T-1, Transfer of Title: itself, its windows, its rainbows and Spout (conditions attached), given to Baron Brume with compliments.

The WELCOME mat, the spare key under it and the fruit basket on Brume's step were always for him. Now he has to keep a castle and 100,000 acres of rainbow on three crowns a month. Spout approves of that, the first festive thing he has ever approved.

outro: The castle considers the matter closed. It is very sorry about all of it.
